manufacturing:
The workshop

Nkpor, Idemili North, Anambra State

The two crafts belong in one group because each is incomplete without the other. Chairs, sofas and beds need a builder before they need a cover, and they need the cover before they can be sold. Run from one workshop they share a supply chain, a delivery fleet and a quality standard — and an institutional buyer can order a complete fit-out, framed and finished, from a single contract.

Most competitors sell furniture or furnishings. The group sells a finished room.

Two crafts, one roof

  • 01 Furniture Desks, chairs, beds, cabinets, doors, joinery. Timber, MDF and plywood — woodworking machines are the core capital item, and the power load is heavy.
  • 02 Soft furnishings Cushions, mattresses, upholstery, curtains, bed linen, rugs. Fabric, foam and thread, moved through Onitsha and Apapa — lighter machinery, and products that turn over faster and are re-ordered more often.

Who it supplies

Institutions first, retail second

Schools

Classroom and dormitory furniture, tendered through the Anambra State Universal Basic Education Board, with the bedding and drapery that goes with it.

Offices

Desks and storage, upholstered seating and window treatments.

Hospitals and clinics

Furniture, bedding, curtains and screens.

Hotels and hospitality

Complete room fit-outs — the highest-volume repeat order in the sector.

Why it lasts

Every piece is built from kiln-dried timber. Air-dried and green timber — what most workshops in Anambra use — warps, cracks and degrades within three to five years. It is the single biggest cause of furniture failure in the market, and the reason institutions will pay more for what lasts.

Foam and fabric are verified rather than assumed, because in soft furnishings the filling and the weave are what fail first, and neither is visible in the finished piece.

Materials and power

Timber comes from Niger Delta hardwoods and from Cross River and Ondo plantations through Onitsha merchants; MDF and plywood are imported through Apapa; foam, fabric and thread move through Onitsha. Power is solved independently of the grid, because woodworking is a heavy load and a workshop that stops when the grid does cannot hold an institutional contract.

Where this stands

This is the group's manufacturing business, and it is the one being started. The workshop is not yet built. What the group has today is Ozi Ikoro, Ozituma and OmaPolo, and the Record says so.

The group's other projects — the Ozi Ikoro museum and agriculture — are on Projects.

02 · Planning

Ozi Ikoro

Awka, Anambra State

A museum, art gallery and anthropological research hub in a converted warehouse.

The name is the purpose: Ozi Ikoro — “Message of the Drum”. The museum speaks, communicating history and identity through objects, images and scholarship.

The concept is deliberately two-sided: the intellectual depth of a museum with the commercial energy of a gallery, so that preservation funds itself. Around the galleries sit a research library and archive, a digital theatre, and a conservation laboratory the public can watch.

The Artefacts“Footprints in Red Earth” — historical objects shown in small rotating groups under single-object lighting, in silence.
The Art“The Future of Form” — a commercial gallery for contemporary Nigerian artists, showing solo and group exhibitions.
The Mixed“Drawing and Object” — nineteenth-century sketches hung beside the tools and objects they depict, so the visitor sees how Igbo life was drawn and what it was drawn with.
The archiveA climate-controlled library and archive of Igbo and south-east Nigerian studies: rare books, early ethnographic works, missionary publications in Igbo, maps, and oral history recordings.
The digital theatreHistoric film of Igboland — colonial film unit archives, early ethnographic footage and broadcast archives — shown on a decoder wall with individual viewing stations.
The conservation laboratoryGlass-walled and visible from the main path: cleaning, cataloguing and preservation done where visitors can see it.

03 · Planning

Ezeme Agriculture

The Idemmili belt and Nkpor

Production where the land is cheap; processing where the market is.

Production sits in the Idemmili belt, where land is affordable. Processing sits at Nkpor, which is too valuable to farm — the same site as the group's headquarters, with storage, packaging and quality control alongside.

ProductionPrimary crop production on Idemmili land, developed as a working farm rather than a land holding.
ProcessingAn agro-processing line for staples — cassava and rice products, palm oil, milled flour — with a cold storage hub, a packaging unit and a quality-control laboratory.
Why it belongs to the groupThe furniture and soft furnishings businesses fund land acquisition. Agriculture is the use the land is bought for.
